question: A membership officer asked Claude for the wording of a renewal reminder that her team will revise repeatedly over the next few weeks before sending it. Claude returned it as an ordinary reply in the chat. What should she do first?
options: A) Copy the wording into the team's chat channel so that colleagues can suggest changes there.
B) Ask Claude to put the wording into an artifact that the team can go on editing and reusing.
C) Ask Claude for several more versions of the wording and pick between them at a later point.
D) Paste the wording into a fresh conversation each time the team wants to change something.
correct_answers: B) Ask Claude to put the wording into an artifact that the team can go on editing and reusing.
explanations: A chat channel scatters revisions across messages with no single current version, which is the problem she is trying to avoid over several weeks of editing.

Correct. Content that is self-contained, will be iterated on, and is meant to be reused outside the conversation is what an artifact is for. Putting the reminder in one gives the team a single editable version to work on rather than a reply buried in chat history.
More variants add choice, not durability. The team would still be editing text that lives inside a conversation and has to be found again each time.
Starting a new conversation for every change loses the context behind earlier edits and produces a trail of near-identical drafts with no authoritative copy.
